chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Husayn ibn Hashim and Ali ibn Ribat and Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a man who sells for a group of people, with the condition that his liability covers their property. He said: 'If his soul is pleased with that, I only fear that they will impose upon him more than he gains from them. But if his soul is pleased with it, there is no harm.'

key_terms.طَابَتْ نَفْسُهُ: His soul was pleased (contentment with the risk/condition)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on a broker guaranteeing the property of his clients?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) permits the broker (simsar) to act as a guarantor (*daman*) for the goods he sells, provided the clients consent willingly. The Imam highlights the practical risk of this arrangement, noting that the broker may end up liable for losses exceeding his commission, thus emphasizing the importance of clear mutual agreement in commercial transactions. This ruling reflects the Shia juristic principle of allowing flexibility in trade contracts (*mu'amalat*) as long as there is no explicit prohibition or deception.
